en: (Singing)

This song is almost 900 years old. It was written by Comtessa de Dia, a poet and composer from medieval southern France. It is the only surviving melody written by a woman from that entire tradition. So let me start with the question: who decides which voices survive? I never really thought about that until a few years ago, when I was working in a second-hand book market in London, and I found an encyclopedia that listed 6,000 women composers in the history of music. I could not believe it because at that time I think I could name five. But as soon as I started looking into their names and listening to this incredible music, I kid you not, I would not shut up. Well I haven’t shut up. I’m here. And I just am sharing this music with everybody all the time. In fact, please allow me.
(Music)
I mean, can you believe that? Did you hear all the classical strings? The Afro-American dances mixed with the romantic music? Well welcome to my husband’s life in 2018.
(Laughter)
Now, my husband, he’s a railway engineer, which means he's now the railway engineer who knows the most about women composers in the whole world.
(Laughter)
I know, it's not a very competitive field, but still.
(Laughter)

So one day he said to me, "Look, it's very nice that you're playing this music by these women at breakfast for like, I don't know, a year now. But you do understand that nothing is going to happen if you just tell me. I'm an engineer. So are you going to do something or what?" And I was like, "Fair enough." So I did. I made a list of these incredible women. I put it online, and within months, women from all over the world started writing to me and they said, "Thank you so much for what you're doing. I'm a composer. Could you please add me to your list?" And I tell you, this list continues to grow. It is now a foundation, and we are now uncovering over 18,000 women composers in the history of music.
(Applause)

Now this story makes absolutely no sense. I'm a professional musician. How is it possible that I spent my life training and performing without hearing about thousands of women who wrote beautiful music? Well when I started doing my own research, and I came across the data, then it became clear because, it turns out, that nearly 90 percent of the music we hear across genres is written by men. That's a very big gap. Can you imagine all the amazing music we've been all missing all this time? But also that AI is now learning from that same silence. On one platform only, more than 50,000 AI-generated tracks are added every single day. The systems can only learn from the data available to them, but right now that data is missing. Half of humanity's creativity. Now I believe musicians should be writing music, not machines.
(Applause)
There are millions of talented people who can do that. Writing music fills our soul ... as humans. And to generate music from artists' work without their consent or proper remuneration is wrong.
(Applause and cheers)

But the technology is here to stay. So let's make sure all voices are heard, right? So how do we do that? It's actually quite easy. We must record the missing voices -- the historical ones, but also the current ones who are not represented. Because a recording makes this music searchable, teachable, and part of the systems shaping what the world will hear next. It brings this music to classrooms, to radio stations, to streaming platforms so everybody in this room can play and share it. So here's my invitation. What if every tech company making AI music and anyone profiting from it would invest in making our musical catalog more complete? Can you imagine? What gets heard is chosen, and those choices will shape what the future will remember. So who decides which voices survive? Now more than ever, we do.

And I want to leave you all with one woman's story. Ilse Weber was a poet, a singer who was imprisoned in the ghetto of Theresienstadt during World War II with her family. As she was there, she didn't write symphonies, but she wrote songs to entertain the elderly and the children. That's the power of music. And that was the gift of one woman. She and her son sadly died in Auschwitz, but her husband buried her manuscripts under a tool shed, and because of that, a few of her songs survived. This one is a lullaby. It's called "Wiegala".
(Singing)
(Song stops abruptly) [If you can’t hear this part, perhaps history never recorded it.] Artificial intelligence is learning. Let's teach it to remember the sounds of all of us.
Thank you.
(Applause)

I've been writing about global health and medical innovation for years, and when I tell my friends and family how much progress there's been, the reaction is almost always the same. They had no idea most of it was happening. Take the most common cause of death today, heart disease. People today have roughly a quarter the chance of dying from heart disease as people did in the 1950s at the same age. A quarter. Back then, there were no statins, no cholesterol testing, no implanted pacemakers, no anti-smoking campaigns, no bans on trans fats, no bypass surgery, no CPR. But hardly anyone hears about the long-term impact of those breakthroughs. When progress happens gradually, it's rarely considered news. And I think it's a problem. I think it’s part of why people don’t know how important it’s all been -- public health, vaccines and all the rest -- in improving people’s lives. But what I want to tell you about is the thing that doesn't make the news at all. Not the breakthroughs themselves, but everything that got in the way of them.

I used to have this impression that breakthroughs were uncommon, sporadic, sometimes happening by pure chance, sometimes by sheer determination. The way I see it now, it's more like there's a continuous stream of medical innovation every year. In just the last two years, for example, we've had a new antiviral against HIV, which protects against infections with an efficacy of nearly 100 percent with just a single dose given every six months. There are new drugs that reduce cholesterol levels by 60 percent, beyond the effect of statins. There are new treatments that slow down the progression of certain cancers, certain lung cancers, brain cancer and multiple myeloma by half or more. And in just the last five years, we've had new vaccines against four diseases for the very first time. COVID, of course, but also the first malaria vaccine, the first chikungunya vaccine and the first vaccine against RSV.

The tools to develop new drugs and vaccines have improved enormously. Like genome sequencing, for example, which has touched almost every part of biology. Back when the Human Genome Project was completed in 2003, it cost $50 million to sequence one person’s genome, and it took half a year. Now it takes under four hours and it costs a few hundred dollars. There's also been a revolution in the technology of microscopes. Over the past 200 years, their resolution has increased over 10,000-fold. We can now see viruses down to their individual atoms and design new drugs to target them extremely precisely. This is RSV, respiratory syncytial virus. It's in the middle right there. And we can now see its atomic structure on the right. Until the 1930s, no one had ever seen a virus. So if our technology has advanced so much, why are so many diseases still untreatable today?

What I've learned is that technology isn't always the barrier. Sometimes it’s about the funding, the institutions and the incentives. We recently got a new malaria vaccine, as I mentioned, and when I first heard about it, I was amazed. I remember learning that malaria was a very complicated disease, scientifically. It's caused by a parasite, not a virus or bacterium. And that parasite changes shape multiple times during its life cycle, which makes it really hard to know what to target with a vaccine. So I wanted to write about it, this amazing breakthrough. But one of the first things I learned about this new malaria vaccine that was introduced just a few years ago, was that it was developed in the '90s. Decades ago. The researchers who developed it, struggled to find funding to test it at every stage of the process. There was no commercial incentive. It's not profitable to develop new drugs and vaccines against diseases that affect people in poverty, in poorer countries, even if millions of children might benefit. Even if there’s a huge economic benefit as well. It took foreign aid and philanthropy to fund the research to test it. And it literally took decades to reach the children who needed it. When I learned about this, I felt like there was nothing to celebrate. It seemed more like a failure. How could we let that happen? How could it take so long to test a vaccine that had already been developed, while half a million children were dying from malaria every year? Why wasn't that the story?

Those children aren't coming back. But what I wanted to know was how we could prevent that from happening again. Like, what if we could change the economic incentives? Well, economists have come up with an idea to do just that. It’s called an “advanced market commitment.” It's where donors commit to buying a vaccine at a certain price per dose, but only if it's developed and proven safe and effective. That commitment gives companies the confidence to invest in it in the first place, and it can bring vaccines into existence that would otherwise never get made. And most importantly, it makes sure that they're manufactured at scale and sold at an affordable price, so they reach children who need them.

That idea was used over a decade ago to help develop new vaccines against pneumococcal disease, which is a deadly bacterial infection of the lungs. Vaccines already existed, but they didn't include the strains that were common in Africa and South Asia. So in 2009, several countries and philanthropists came together to fund an advanced market commitment for new vaccines. And it actually worked. Several companies developed them, and they reached children much faster than usual. It's estimated that those vaccines have saved over 700,000 children's lives since then.
(Applause)

This idea to fix market incentives is one way to speed up the process. But it's not the only thing we can do. Take childhood leukemia, for example. It used to be very difficult to test new treatments for the disease because leukemia is rare and individual hospitals struggled to find enough patients to run clinical trials. So researchers built networks across the US and later Europe and Canada to help recruit patients from all over those countries into larger clinical trials. That collaboration made it possible to test treatments and learn what works faster. And it's why leukemia is no longer the disease it used to be. Before the 1970s, only around 15 percent of children with leukemia would survive even five years from a diagnosis. That's the bottom line on these graphs. Two types of leukemia. Now the top line -- that figure is 85 percent. Most children in richer countries today survive and are effectively cured of the disease. This graph is thousands of children who wouldn't have survived without that collaboration, without that progress.

I want to give you another example. Back when I was at university, we had a substitute lecturer one day in my course on infectious diseases, and she told us that our original lecturer was away because he had gone to West Africa to do research to develop an Ebola vaccine. I remember sitting in that lecture theater at the back, and I was thinking to myself, can you just do that? Can you just pack up and go? It hadn't even occurred to me, and it made me realize that all of these breakthroughs came from people like him, people who changed their lives to make them happen, or people who thought differently, whether they were scientists, economists, operators or managers. They created the incentives and institutions so that generations in the future, all of us, wouldn't have to face the same problems that they did. And what's amazing is that we have an Ebola vaccine now against the most common strain. It wasn't made by my lecturer, but by researchers like him. And it was hard to develop and test it for all the same reasons. There was little commercial incentive, and it was hard to run clinical trials because it was hard to predict where Ebola outbreaks would arise and vaccinate people in advance. So scientists came up with a different idea. They waited for individual cases of Ebola to appear and then quickly vaccinated all of the people around them [and] tested the vaccine that way. That idea, called ring vaccination, helped find a vaccine that we now know is very effective.

Now these are just some of the ideas that people have had so far. But what I've learned from them is that breakthroughs don't just happen because we have the tools to make them. They depend on how innovation happens in the real world. And there's something else that I've learned from them that I find much harder to stomach. Many of them might not have happened at all. So when I think back to that stream of innovation, all of those breakthroughs and all of that progress that we've seen, I do find it amazing. It's incredible. But it also really frustrates me. That's how much progress we've made despite it being so hard. The good news is people have come up with ideas to change that. Some of them really work, like the ones I've told you about today, and they just haven't been used enough. But we also need people to come up with new ideas and test them and scale them up too. I think it's more important than ever that we do it, because of cuts to science, global health and foreign aid, we have to find ways to make our resources go further.

Progress isn't inevitable. It takes people who decide to persist despite that. And I think here it takes people who recognize something quite simple. That diseases are not a fact of life. They're problems that we can solve.
Thank you.
(Applause)

The internet is an absolute miracle. And for the last 30 years, it has been driven by [a] very consistent and fundamental business model that has given us everything amazing about the internet and everything not so amazing as well. I run a company that provides a lot of the internet's infrastructure and as a result, means three things. One, we've had this unique view into what is going on online. Two, we care enormously about the success of the internet. And three, I can share with you some of how that underlying business model is changing and why it's important. Because as that business model changes, it's going to have a dramatic impact on what the internet is, but beyond that, on what content is created, on what journalists get compensated for, on how researchers are able to do their research. And so it's up to all of us as that business model of the internet changes, to make sure it changes for something we want and can learn from the mistakes that we had in the past.

So to review the past, let's look at what that business model was. And we all know it basically, which was: the internet was built on we took an idea, and we put it online, and then we drove traffic to that idea. And then from that traffic, we either sold things, subscriptions or ads. And it's been pretty amazing to watch how that has very much driven the growth of the web and the growth of the internet over time. And it survived a number of dramatic platform shifts. We all started browsing the internet on browsers, on our desktop or laptop. That transitioned to be increasingly social media, which was the interface through which we consumed content. And then we went to consuming it through our mobile devices. And yet, through all of this, the humble banner ad has basically financed it all. Traffic has been the currency of the internet, and that's what everyone has built their content to try to achieve.

And if we want to look for who's the Superman, who's the superhero that has driven this for the last 27 years, that has been Google. Google built not only the search engine to index how the internet works, but then they built the monetization system to actually ensure that content creators got paid for the traffic that they generated. The internet owes a ton to Google in the last 27 years. But the world is changing. AI is the topic du jour, and what I think a lot of people don't understand is that AI is yet another platform shift. Think about how much more of the way that you consume information already is looking at your AI chatbot, and how much more of that will be the case in the future. We can see it in a lot of things we do kind of normally, like, this is a Google search from the early days of Google. Not even that long ago, where I would type something in, like, when was the first TED conference? And then I would get back basically a treasure map where I would have to continue to do the work and click on the links, generating traffic to find what my answer was. The search wasn't over when the results returned. That was just the beginning, and you had to follow the treasure map. That's what a search engine is.

Today we have something very different. We have something that's closer to what I would call an answer engine, where you're getting the answer directly on the page. And what's amazing about that is that as a consumer, it's better for you. But what's terrifying about it is that it means traffic isn't going to the publishers' sites, and traffic is the currency of the internet. And so 18 months ago, publishers called us and said, “Are you seeing this, too?” And I have to confess, we weren't really paying a ton of attention, but we went into our logs, we went into our data, we pulled out that information and said, “How much harder is it to get traffic based on the same amount of content today than it was with the Google of old?” And the answer is, it's 5.2 times harder to get traffic for the same amount of content that was out there. But that's the good news. That's with Google. What is it with OpenAI? 750 times harder. What is it with Anthropic? 32,000 times harder. The answer engines are giving the answers and people aren't following the footnotes. And this was 18 months ago. What’s happened since, has it gotten better or worse? Do you trust AI more today than you did 18 months ago? The answer is most people do, and as a result, it's actually gotten twice as hard to get traffic to content that's there. You're not following the footnotes anymore. You're actually trusting that AI systems are giving you the right answer, and that's destroying media.

Across the board, we're seeing reported numbers ... of between a 90 and 30 percent decline in the traffic to their sites, and this is extremely problematic because I think journalists deserve to be able to eat.
(Applause)

And fundamentally, if the internet is built on traffic and this new business model isn't delivering traffic, then I'm not sure how media is going to survive unless we create a new business model. And the good news is the AI companies want journalism. They want people out there doing research. We all want journalism. We want people out there doing research. And so I think, I'm actually kind of optimistic that there might be a solution to this problem. And here's the way I think about it.

For the first time in human history, we have a mathematical model of all of human knowledge. It's not perfect, but that's essentially what all of the LLMs are. And I think of it like a giant block of Swiss cheese. There's a lot of cheese, that's what we know. But we also have a lot of holes in the cheese. Those are the things we don't know. And the thing that is incredible is that what all of you want, what I want, what the AI companies want is they want people out there filling in the holes in the cheese. They don’t want you writing stories that already exist -- they want you actually creating new knowledge. And the AI companies, I've talked to every one of them, they're all willing to actually pay for people who are creating new knowledge, creating new ideas, ideas worth spreading. That's what this new system would reward. Compare that to what the business model of media is for the last 10 years, which is not filling in the holes in the cheese, but instead, basically, lighting the cheese on fire, right? Incendiary cheese, right? Yet another story about what happened at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, told in the most inflammatory way possible. I've sat with media executives who brag about the fact that they create content for as little as possible, and then write headlines that create the largest cortisol response so that you will click on them. That's not a world we should be celebrating. That's not a world that's making the world better. If, on the other hand, we actually celebrated who is making the cheese bigger, who's filling in that --

Imagine in the future that you actually had AI companies that were measuring who actually advanced human knowledge mathematically over the course of the last year the most, and we gave them an award. We could call it the Big Cheese award.
(Laughter)

I'm not kidding. Like, how amazing would that be? And you might be thinking, OK, Matthew, you're crazy. Like, I'm the person who thinks AI is just destroying the world, and technology always makes things worse. I'm going to share just two anecdotes that make me have some hope that this might actually be the case. The first starts 23 years ago.

23 years ago, the music industry had a huge problem: Napster, Kazaa -- everyone was stealing music. And then Steve Jobs stepped on stage, almost 23 years ago to this day, and he said, “We’re going to do something different. We're going to charge 99 cents per song. We're going to actually say that you should be paying for the music that you consume.” Now that’s not the business model that won, but it was the start, and it turned into what is today Spotify and all the other systems that are out there, which is basically $10 a month, all-you-can-eat music, and it's pretty amazing. Last year, Spotify alone sent over $10 billion to music creators in revenue. And again, that's in addition to titles, TikToks, YouTube, Apple Music, everybody else, more money is going to music creation than any time in human history. So technology can be pie-expanding. In fact, I thought it was so important that I flew up to Stockholm to meet with Daniel Ek, the founder of Spotify, and he said, "You know, it's pretty amazing. We know when someone goes to Spotify and they type in Taylor Swift, "Shake It Off" that we can give them what they're looking for." But every once in a while, someone comes in and types in something like, 'I want a song about how much fun it is to dance disco with your cat.'
(Laughter)

And nobody's written that. But they know that nobody's written that. And so they actually go back and take those queries and then publish them back to music creators. And this is the moment you're all going to think you're doing life wrong. But there's a guy who lives in Denmark who makes €40 million a year writing songs for unfulfilled Spotify queries.
(Laughter)

And I think that's beautiful. That's filling the holes in the cheese. Because when I look for a song, what I'm looking for is an emotion. And this person is helping me find a song to resonate that way. And I think that's a model for what could happen as well.

Another story starts a little bit closer to home. So this is the Park Record newspaper. The first place I ever saw my name in print -- my hometown newspaper from Park City, Utah. It was dying. So three years ago, my wife and I bought it. We did not buy it because we thought it was going to be a great business. We bought it because we thought local news was important. In fact, we had no financial KPIs -- the only KPI we focused on was how much could we increase voter turnout. And the answer was, we got it from the low 20 percent to over 60 percent in the last election in three years, which is amazing, right?
(Applause)

Local news matters. But here's the crazy part. Terrible business, right? Except it's not. We're likely going to make more in 2026 off licensing our content to AI companies than we do off digital advertising. Why? Because if you're traveling to Park City, Utah, and you want to know what's the great new restaurant, what's the cool band that's coming to town, we're the only ones that have it. So think about how amazing that would be.

Think about how if in the future, the business model of the new AI-driven internet actually rewards the media we're all craving, local, unique, original content. That's what I'm super excited about. But there are problems. Challenges. It's kind of like in the superhero films, where the hero of the last movie becomes the villain of the next. And so our good friends at Google ... Ugh.
(Laughter)

They are holding this back. They believe that they have a God-given right to all of the content online. They shouldn't have to pay for any of it. And they have a huge advantage. In fact, it's hard to believe this, but every other AI company was actually started to oppose Google, right? That’s what OpenAI started with. Anthropic was just a spinoff of OpenAI, xAI. All of this was all to say, we can't let Google win this entire game. How much of an advantage do they have? Well we looked at this again, and we found that every single page that OpenAI sees, Google sees three. Four in Microsoft’s case, five in Anthropic's case, 21 or 22 in xAI's case. An enormous advantage that Google has, and they want to hold on to that advantage. In fact, they're playing incredibly dirty. They're saying to content creators, "You can't stop us from training on your content or we will take you out of search." Horrible. Superman, how far you’ve fallen!
(Laughter)

And so I was pretty depressed, I have to confess, thinking we were on the cusp of creating something amazing: a better internet. And yet, I have to just realize that no AI company's top priority is paying content creators. What's their top priority? Beating Google. Which gave me an idea. Kind of a wonderful idea. An idea which is going on right now, and it's working.

Which is: don’t charge for all the content that’s out there, just charge the AI companies for the ability to catch Google. And I don't think that's the end game, but I think it might be the iTunes moment. It might be the point that shows us content is worth paying for. Everyone should be out there, and we can create a better business model for the internet. And so I'm hopeful that on this stage, not too long from now, I get to hand out one of the first Big Cheese awards, and I really appreciate it.
Thank you.
zh: 互联网绝对是一个奇迹。 在过去的 30 年中， 它一直采用同一种基本商业模式， 为我们带来了互联网的喜人之处， 也有不喜人之处。 我经营的公司提供 大量的互联网基础设施， 这就意味着三件事。 第一，我们对于线上发生了什么 有着独特的视角。 第二，我们非常关心互联网的成功。 第三，我可以和大家分享一下 底层商业模式发生了什么变化， 为何如此重要。 因为随着商业模式的变化， 它将对互联网的本质产生巨大影响， 但除此之外，还会影响内容的创作、 记者获得的报酬、 研究人员的研究能力。 因此，我们都有责任 在互联网的商业模式发生变化时， 确保它向着我们想要的方向改变， 并从过去的错误中吸取教训。

说到回顾过去，我们来看看 曾经的商业模式是什么样的。 我们其实都知道，互联网基于 我们将一个想法发到网上， 再为这个想法吸引流量。 借助这些流量，我们出售商品、 订阅或者广告。 见证这种模式如何刺激网络的逐步增长、 互联网的逐步增长真是太神奇了。 这种模式也在屡次 剧烈的平台更替中保留了下来。 一开始，我们在浏览器、台式机 或笔记本电脑上浏览互联网。 然后是越来越多的社交媒体， 也就是我们消费内容的交互媒介。 然后我们通过移动设备消费内容。 但是，所有这些互动， 都由这个不起眼的横幅广告提供资金。 流量是互联网的货币， 这也是每个人创作内容的目的所在。

如果我们想找出谁是超人， 谁是过去 27 年里 推动这一切的超级英雄， 那就是谷歌。 谷歌不仅建立了搜索引擎， 索引互联网的运作方式， 还建立了变现系统， 确保内容创作者 能从他们产生的流量中获得报酬。 在过去的 27 年中， 互联网在很大程度上要归功于谷歌。 但是世界正在发生变化。 AI 是当今的话题， 我想很多人还没发现 AI 也是一场平台更替。 想想你消费信息的方式 有多少已经变成了 AI 聊天机器人， 将来还会出现多少这样的情况。 我们可以从很多 习以为常的行为中看出这一点， 比如，这是谷歌早期的谷歌搜索。 不久以前， 我会输入一些内容， 比如第一届 TED 大会是什么时候？ 然后我会得到一张藏宝图， 我得继续探索， 点击链接，产生流量， 才能找到我的答案。 结果返回时，搜索尚未结束。 那只是开始，你还得顺着藏宝图去找。 这就是搜索引擎。

如今，我们有了截然不同的东西。 我会觉得更接近“答案引擎”， 直接在页面上得到答案。 好处是对于消费者更好。 但可怕的是， 这代表流量不会流向发布者的网站， 而流量是互联网的货币。 18 个月前，发布者给我们打电话 说：“你也看到了吗？” 我必须承认， 我们没有太关注这些， 但是我们打开了日志，查看了数据， 提取了信息，然后说： “现在要基于如今的内容量产生流量， 要比当时的谷歌难多少？” 答案是，基于同等内容量 获取同等流量要难 5.2 倍。 但这算是个好消息。 谷歌是这个数字。 OpenAI 是多少？ 750 倍的难度。 Anthropic 是多少？ 32,000 倍的难度。 答案引擎直接给出答案， 人们不会点进标注的来源页。 那是 18 个月前的事了。 之后呢？更好了，还是更坏了？ 比起 18 个月以前， 你现在更信任 AI 吗？ 答案是大多数人更信任了， 于是为内容产生流量的难度翻了一番。 你再也不会点进标注页。 你真的相信 AI 系统会给出正确的答案， 而这正在摧毁媒体。
总体而言，我们看到的数字是 网站流量出现 90% 到 30% 的下降， 问题很严重， 因为我觉得记者得有饭吃。
（掌声）
归根结底， 如果互联网建立在流量之上， 而这种新的商业模式无法提供流量， 那么我不知道媒体该如何生存， 除非我们创造一个新型商业模式。 好消息是，AI 公司想要新闻业。 他们希望有人出去做研究。 我们都想要新闻业。 我们希望有人出去做研究。 因此我认为， 我对这个问题其实是乐观的， 这个问题会有答案的。 我是这么想的。

我们在人类历史上首次 有了一个涵盖所有人类知识的数学模型。 它并不完美， 但这就是 LLM（大语言模型）的本质。 我觉得它就像一大块瑞士奶酪。 奶酪的部分很多， 这代表我们知道的东西。 但奶酪上也有很多洞， 这代表我们不知道的东西。 不可思议的是 你们都想要的、我想要的、 AI 公司想要的 都是有人可以填满奶酪上的洞。 他们不想让你写已经存在的故事， 他们希望你创造新知识。 而 AI 公司，每家我都聊过了， 他们都愿意为那些创造新知识、 创造新想法、值得传播的想法的人买单。 这就是这个新系统奖励的东西。 对比媒体过去 10 年的商业模式， 并非填满奶酪的洞， 而是点燃奶酪，对吧？ 着火的奶酪，对吧？ 宾夕法尼亚大道 1600 号 发生过一个故事， 叙述方式最具煽动性。 我曾与媒体高管坐下聊过， 他们夸夸其谈写出一丁点内容， 再写出最能引起皮质醇反应的标题， 吸引你去点击。 我们不该歌颂这样的世界。 这不能让世界更美好。 如果我们反而能歌颂 那些把奶酪做得更大、 把奶酪填满的人……
想象一下，未来 AI 公司 从数学上衡量过去一年 谁最多地拓展了人类知识， 再授予奖项。 我们可以称之为“大奶酪奖”。
（笑声）
我不是在开玩笑。 这多棒啊！ 你可能会想，马修，你疯了。 我认为 AI 就是在毁灭世界， 科技总是让情况变得更糟。 我想分享两件轶事，让我有了一些希望， 也许能有改观。 第一件事是 23 年前。

23 年前，音乐行业 遇到了一个巨大的问题： Napster、 Kazaa， 人人都在偷音乐。 然后史蒂夫·乔布斯登上舞台， 差不多至今 23 年前。 他说：“我们的做法不一样。 我们将为每首歌收取 99 美分的费用。 我们的意思就是 你得为你消费的音乐花钱。” 这不是胜出的商业模式， 但是个起点，才有了今天的 Spotify 和市面上的各种系统， 每月 10 美元畅听， 非常棒。 去年，仅 Spotify 就向音乐创作者带来了 超过 100 亿美元的收入。 这还不包括 TIDAL、TikTok、YouTube， 苹果音乐等等各种平台， 人类历史上音乐创作从未赚过这么多钱。 科技能让我们把蛋糕做得更大。 我觉得飞到斯德哥尔摩与 Spotify 创始人丹尼尔· 埃克会面非常重要， 他说：“太神奇了。 我们知道用户在 Spotify 里 输入泰勒·斯威夫特， ‘Shake It Off’， 他们就能得到想要的结果。” 但总有人时不时输入类似 “有一首和我的猫蹦迪的歌该多好玩啊。”
（笑声）
没人写过这样的歌。 但他们也知道没人写过这样的歌。 于是他们会拿着这些关键词， 发回给音乐创作者。 此时此刻你会感叹还有这种活法。 但是有一个住在丹麦的人， 每年赚 4000 万欧元， 为搜不到的 Spotify 关键词写歌。
（笑声）
太美妙了。 这就是填上奶酪的洞。 因为我在找一首歌时， 我要找的其实是一种情感。 这个人能帮我找到产生这种共鸣的歌曲。 我认为这可以是一个未来的样板。

另一个故事离我家比较近。 这是 The Park Record 报纸。 我第一次在印刷品上见到我的名字， 来自我的家乡犹他州帕克城的报纸。 这家媒体已经要关门了。 三年前，我和妻子买下了它。 我们买它并不是因为 我们觉得是个好生意。 我们买它是因为我们认为 本地新闻很重要。 我们并没有财务上的绩效指标， 我们关注的唯一绩效指标 就是增加了多少选民投票率。 结果是在三年内，在上一次选举中， 投票率从 20% 低值升至 60% 以上， 太厉害了，对吧？
（掌声）
本地新闻很重要。 令人意外的地方来了。 赔本买卖，对吧？ 实则并非。 到 2026 年，我们通过 将内容授权给 AI 公司的收入 可能会超过数字广告 获得的收入。为什么？ 因为如果你要去犹他州帕克城旅行， 想知道有哪家很棒的新餐厅， 城里要来什么厉害的乐队， 只有我们知道。 想想有多神奇吧。
想一想，如果将来， AI 驱动的新互联网的商业模式 真的会奖励我们都渴望的媒体， 提供本地、独特的原创内容。 我对此十分期待。 但是有些问题。 挑战。 有点像超级英雄电影中， 上一部电影的英雄 变成了下一部电影的反派。 那么我们在谷歌的好朋友们…… 呃。
（笑声）

他们不会接受这些。 他们相信他们拥有上帝赋予 掌管所有在线内容的权利。 他们也无需为此付费。 而且他们有巨大的优势。 难以置信， 但其他 AI 公司都开始抵制谷歌，对吧？ OpenAI 就是这么起家的。 Anthropic 只是 OpenAI 的衍生，还有 xAI。 这些都是在说明， 我们不能让谷歌称霸一切。 他们有多少优势？ 我们重新看一看， 会发现 OpenAI 每看到一页， 谷歌能看到三页。 是微软的四倍。 Anthropic 的五倍， xAI 的 21 或 22 倍。 这是谷歌拥有的巨大优势， 他们也希望保持这一优势。 但他们手段非常肮脏。 他们对内容创作者说： “你们无法阻止 我们利用你们的内容训练， 不然我们就让别人搜不到你们。” 太可怕了。 超人，你太堕落了！
（笑声）
我不得不承认， 我当时非常沮丧， 以为我们差点就要创造出 这么棒的东西了—— 更好的互联网。 但是，我必须意识到， 没有哪家 AI 公司的首要任务 是向内容创作者付费。 他们的首要任务是什么？ 击败谷歌。 让我有了一个主意。 真是个好主意。 这个想法现在正在发生，也是有用的。
那就是： 不要为所有现有内容收费， 而是向 AI 公司收取赶上谷歌的费用。 我不认为一切都玩完了， 但我认为这可能是个 iTunes 时刻。 这可能是展现“内容值得付费”的时刻。 每个人都该参与， 我们可以为互联网创造更好的商业模式。 我希望在这个舞台上，不久之后， 我能颁发第一批“大奶酪奖”， 非常感谢。
谢谢。

en: By the year 2030, nearly half of all the young people walking this earth will be African. And being able to read is the scale upon which so many other skills depend. Yet, more than 80 percent of 10-year-old children in sub-Saharan Africa cannot read a simple text with understanding. Not because they're not smart, not because they didn't pitch up for school, but because the system is failing them. The go-to solution for this learning crisis has always been the same: build more schools, build more classrooms, hire more teachers, train more teachers. Sounds reasonable. But here’s the uncomfortable truth no one really wants to say out loud: It's actually never going to work. To meet ideal student-to-teacher ratios, sub-Saharan Africa needs 15 million more teachers at a staggering cost of almost $40 billion a year. It's just nuts. So why are we still holding on to a playbook that cannot possibly deliver at the cost and urgency and scale required?

Well, it's because we have a weird bias. Not that kind of weird, but a WEIRD bias -- the idea, the assumption that solutions that work in countries that are Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic should somehow work everywhere else in the world.
(Applause)

The assumption that WEIRD countries are the standard, "the way the world works," and somehow with more inputs, African schools should eventually look like WEIRD ones. Let's pause right there, because that assumption is at the heart of the problem. And God knows so many others. We shouldn't have to frame our world like that. And I certainly have outgrown the belief that African schools should fit a borrowed model. Our goal should be to build something brilliant that actually reflects the reality that African children are living in today. At the organization I lead, it’s called “Imagine Worldwide,” we are doing something different. Children like Chisomo, who you will hear about shortly, are now able to experience something else. Chisomo is a typical seven-year-old girl living in rural Malawi with her younger sister and parents who are farmers. It's a pretty happy existence, even without iPhones and ketchup.
(Laughter)

Every morning, she walks through the green maize fields under the glory of the African sun. But at school, she shares a class with a hundred other kids, sometimes 200 -- if a teacher was absent. She can barely see the book that the teacher was holding up in an overcrowded, dimly lit room. She rarely gets a chance to ask a question, share an answer, get feedback -- and feedback is everything. I remember when I tutored high-school math, some kids didn’t even get their marked tests back -- just a score. So they never knew where they went wrong or right, for that matter. There was no feedback loop, just this vacuum of uncertainty that makes it impossible to get better at anything. And [at] Imagine, we are giving children like Chisomo up to an hour a day of high-impact learning on a tablet. I know, I know, I can feel the parents in the room cringing. We are so allergic to the idea of screens, they are bad for mental health, hurting attention spans. Really not good for your mental and emotional development. I get that, and that's all true. In a few contexts. And this is why context is so important.

Chisomo is not living the WEIRD childhood that so many of us are trying to protect our children from. Her reality is not too much tech. It's more closer to none at all, at school or at home. The solution that we are delivering is really designed to tackle some of the hardest things that EdTech has not been able to deliver in Africa. And I know that many of you are very skeptical about tech in poor countries. Our solution is tackling those issues head on. All those prior failures that were too hardware-focused relied on power and connectivity. The ones that were cultural misfits, lacking in sound pedagogy, working outside government systems, or just plain too expensive to run. All of those, we have figured out a model that works. Ready to hear it?
(Cheers and applause)

Specially designed tablets that are solar-charged are used throughout the school day, and they're designed with a battery that can carry over and they can be rotated throughout classes. The content is contextually relevant and delivered in local languages like Swahili and Chichewa, including verbal instruction via the headphones. And it works entirely offline. No internet, no power, no problem. It's not a replacement for teachers, but an extra helping hand. The kids only spend about an hour of their day on it anyway. But in that hour, the tablet does something incredible: It adapts to each child's level and pace, guiding even first-time users, children who are not yet able to read and have never seen a device, from their very first tap, all the way to literacy and numeracy -- without adult intervention.

Imagine what that means in a classroom where individual attention is almost impossible. Each child suddenly gets something incredibly rare: instruction that responds to them. The child who was struggling can slow down and get more practice. The child who is ready to keep going can rush ahead. Imagine in a classroom where 20 kids are each on their own tablets, or 200 -- there is no loss in learning quality. This is all achieved without having to retrain or restructure the entire education system. What we're seeing here is greater access to learning and better learning by the minute. This is unheard of in education. 97 percent of teachers in Malawi have confirmed that the tablet program makes teaching more enjoyable.
(Applause)

And the results speak for themselves. Nine randomized controlled trials across four countries in three languages over the past decade have proven that time-bound, fit-for-context digital learning embedded in public school systems is the most scalable way to accelerate literacy and numeracy outcomes for millions of African children. We are seeing learning gains that rank among the top education interventions anywhere in the world.
(Cheers and applause)
Three years ago, we were already doubling the number of children that become literate and numerate by their fourth year in school. Now we're on track to triple that.
(Applause and cheers)

I think so, too. Beyond test scores, we're seeing more children pitch up and stay in school. Girls catch up and keep pace with boys. And the most important thing, more children are falling in love with learning.

Imagine takes a system- strengthening approach, working in partnership with government from day one to embed the program within public education systems, ensuring a pathway for scale and sustainability. And through that process, we're able to create road maps for others to replicate in more countries in the future.

The best news is this testimony from this innocent girl where she says, "I like the tablet because when I make a mistake, it doesn't move on to the next student. It asks me to try again, and then I can get it right.” Finally, a school experience where children experience success and the dignity of real learning. This year, Imagine will reach one million children.
(Cheers and applause)

And by 2030, thanks to the generosity of this community, we aim to serve over four million children a year across Malawi, Sierra Leone and Tanzania and in the process, create a pathway for many, many others to follow.

This, this right here is how you turn a tide. With a model that can deliver at the scale, quality, cost and urgency required. Imagine a future where foundational learning that is of high quality is democratized, and the majority of every country's children can learn to read so that they too can read to learn and secure a future in skilled work. We don't need to wait. We simply need to act and now. That future is already knocking, sounding the name of every African child.
(Swahili, Chichewa) Thank you.
(Cheers and applause)

As an artist, I want to tell you that AI has completely changed the trajectory of my life. Let me show you into some of my worlds. When some people were focused on productivity and efficiency, I'd been focused on trying to figure out how to incorporate AI into my art. Like a new paintbrush, a canvas, a camera, a music studio, a doorway into my imagination. I’ve worked in film production, fashion and most recently as a graphic designer. But nothing has sparked my curiosity like AI has.

My first images were less “visionary artist” and more, as my friends used to say, "What is that?" But I leaned into the strangeness of the AI, and now it has become my signature style. And I feel like I have a new superpower, and I'm only limited by my imagination, which seems to be endlessly fueled with ideas now. For the first time, the distance between what I imagined and what I could create has closed.

Once AI video was available, I started animating my AI images and making short films. But I felt like something was missing. So I wanted to make my own music to better match the emotion behind my visuals. So I started writing lyrics and using AI to collaborate on the instrumentation. And I draw my inspiration for my lyrics from my visuals or from my life experiences. And I never thought that my music would take on a life of its own. But it has, as I just landed a record deal.
(Applause and Cheers)

Thank you. That feels extraordinary at this chapter of my life. When the music and the visual align perfectly, it can feel like magic. In this next clip I'm going to show you, from my video "Quiet Rebellion", I wrote these lyrics about living as your authentic self and wearing your strange like a crown.

(Song) Let the rhythm be wide and the logic be thin. I'm living in the spaces where the secrets begin. It's a quiet rebellion, a soft kind of war. There'll be somethin' the world hasn't tasted before. There is a fire in the fold, a grace in the strange. I am ink on the page that refuses to change.
(Cheers and Applause)
Thank you. Thank you.

Lately, people have been asking me these same two questions: Is it really art and how do you do it? And this first one's really hard for me to answer, because AI art is brand new, and we're all still trying to figure out where it fits in. And there [are] intense feelings on both sides, and lots of discussion about AI being trained on other artists’ work -- as I was as an art major. But when I sit down to create, there's no other artists' work on my screen. I use references from things in nature, like flowers or insects, patterns, fashion, or whimsical ideas that have been floating around in my head. For me, art is personal. I just want to make things that bring me joy. And if they do the same to someone else, well, maybe that's the definition right there. And how do you do it? Let me take you behind the scenes for a moment.

This image was made in Midjourney using this prompt, "A character in a fairy tale scene in a marketplace, enchanted and cinematic." And it's an OK image. Very AI, nothing at all special. Now here's that exact same prompt using my personalization code and the style reference code. And I've worked really hard to get my images to look like this. A lot of trial and error and time spent training the AI on my personal style and aesthetic. Now, here's a short clip of the final video.

(Song) Welcome to the marketplace where nothing's ever priced the same. You trade your time, you trade your name, you have to laugh. The stalls are built from maybe-so, the cards all say "you'll know, you'll know". You buy a dream, it's buy-one-hope and something extra.
(Applause and Cheers)

Thank you. When AI is guided by human feeling, empathy and intention, it could become something else entirely. You can't explain creativity. You just follow it. But this is what I do know. I started making the best work of my life since I started using AI as a cocreator, and my life has taken off like a rocket ship. Millions of people have found their way to my work through my social sites and music apps. And I feel different, I feel lighter, I feel curious again, and I love using this technology to tell stories that are close to my heart. This next clip is a tribute to older generations and not losing your sense of wonder.
(Music)
(Laughter)
(Song) The restless chase has drifted by, no longer racing for the prize. Now we savor morning's sigh and see new wonder in old eyes.
(Applause)
Thank you.

I feel like we're standing at the beginning of a renaissance, and the possibilities are endless. We haven't even tapped into all of the ways to use AI creatively. And people who have never felt creative a day in their life are trying AI and sparking that creativity for the first time. And that's incredible. So my takeaway for today is if you are curious about AI, try to play a little and make something beautiful or make something strange, but let yourself be surprised by what comes out. But most of all, find your joy.

(Song) I never found a reason why I had to learn to dance. My feet and music found each other. We knew it at first glance. From the moment I could walk my feet just up and ran. When I hear a song, I see a floor, my feet just understand.
Thank you so much. Thank you.
(Applause and Cheers)
